The AI industry just got a new name from Washington—and Elon Musk is already adopting it. President Donald Trump has ordered the federal government to replace “Artificial Intelligence" with "Super Intelligence," and Musk says SpaceXAI will become SpaceXSI.

The unusual rebranding could signal how closely Silicon Valley is aligning itself with Washington’s emerging technology agenda.

Trump Rebrands the Technology

Trump’s Sept. 29 executive order, titled "Inaugurating the Era of Super Intelligence," directs federal agencies to use "Super Intelligence" and "SI" instead of "Artificial Intelligence" and "AI" in official communications, websites, reports and other non-statutory documents.

The order goes further than a branding exercise. It says the administration believes today’s frontier systems have moved beyond the capabilities implied by the term "artificial intelligence" and directs the White House science and technology office to develop a federal definition of "Super Intelligence" within 60 days.

Trump has also created a Super Intelligence Force, led by Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton, to coordinate the government’s efforts to keep the U.S. at the forefront of the technology.

That gives the terminology shift a policy dimension: Washington is trying to frame the next phase of AI development as a strategic national technology race rather than simply another software category.

Read Also: Trump Equates AI Data Centers To 'Oil' But Elides The Facts

Musk Makes It Corporate

Musk was quick to follow.

On Sunday, he confirmed that SpaceXAI, the AI subsidiary of Space Exploration Technologies Corp. (NASDAQ:SPCX), would be renamed SpaceXSI. Musk was responding to an X user who asked whether the company could make the change. "Yes, we will make that change," Musk replied. He also posted: "No more AI. SI. It’s better."

The timing is notable. SpaceXAI itself is relatively new, following the consolidation of Musk’s space and AI businesses. The unit operates Grok and represents a much broader push to integrate AI across Musk’s technology empire.

But investors should distinguish between a terminology change and a business change. Musk has not announced a new product, investment program or technical architecture because of the rebrand.

The significance is instead strategic: Musk is voluntarily adopting language that the Trump administration is trying to make standard across the federal government.

Read Also: Why Elon Musk Thinks AI Is Getting Cheaper, Not Just Smarter

The Bigger AI Trade

That could matter as Washington increasingly treats advanced AI as infrastructure tied to national competitiveness.

The White House says the government has already announced more than $5 billion for the Genesis Mission, aimed at using advanced AI capabilities across science, medicine, energy and manufacturing.

For investors, however, the more important question is whether "Super Intelligence" becomes more than a political label.

The companies benefiting from the AI buildout—Nvidia Corp (NASDAQ:NVDA), Microsoft Corp (NASDAQ:MSFT), Alphabet Inc (NASDAQ:GOOGL)(NASDAQ:GOOG), Meta Platforms Inc (NASDAQ:META) and others—still have to turn increasingly expensive computing infrastructure into revenue and profits.

Musk’s SpaceXSI rebrand may be the first corporate sign that Washington’s language is spreading into Silicon Valley. The investment signal, though, will come from whether the new era brings more government spending, faster deployment and greater demand for the chips and infrastructure powering it.

Arm Holdings Plc. (NASDAQ:ARM) is navigating an escalating legal battle with longtime customer Qualcomm Inc. (NASDAQ:QCOM) while expanding deeper into AI and data center chips, putting the company in increasingly direct competition with some of its traditional licensees.

Arm and Qualcomm returned to U.S. federal court in Delaware on Monday over licensing, technology access and Qualcomm’s relationship with Meta Platforms Inc. (NASDAQ:META). Both stocks traded lower Monday.

• ARM Holdings stock is under selling pressure. What’s pulling ARM shares down?

Qualcomm Challenges Arm’s Licensing Practices

Qualcomm accused Arm of withholding chip-testing tools required under their contract and leaking its 2024 threat to terminate a key license agreement.

Qualcomm claims the leak damaged discussions with Meta over a potential chip deal and is seeking to suspend royalty payments to Arm for up to five years, a remedy potentially worth billions of dollars.

Qualcomm attorney Karen Dunn cited internal documents that she said showed Arm executives referring to Qualcomm as the "enemy" and worrying about declining royalty revenue.

Arm Denies Causing Qualcomm Harm

Arm rejected the allegations and argued that Qualcomm is using litigation to gain leverage in a business dispute.

Arm attorney Gregg LoCascio said Qualcomm failed to demonstrate actual damages.

"They were not harmed in the least," LoCascio said.

Arm also described Qualcomm’s alleged lost chip deals as speculative.

Judge Maryellen Noreika is considering whether Qualcomm can pursue the five-year royalty suspension, which could materially affect Arm if granted.

See More: Top Momentum Stocks

Arm’s Customer Relationships Turn More Competitive

The dispute dates back to Arm’s 2022 lawsuit against Qualcomm. Qualcomm secured a key victory in 2024.

Tensions intensified in March 2025 when Qualcomm filed complaints with regulators in the U.S., Europe and South Korea, alleging that Arm’s push into selling its own chips threatened competition and customer access.

Arm increasingly competes with customers including Qualcomm and NVIDIA Corp. (NASDAQ:NVDA) for AI and data center business, including reported competition to supply Meta with CPUs.

AI Growth Supports Arm Shares

Despite the legal tension, Arm shares have gained close to 180% in 2026, supported by AI infrastructure demand, rising data center CPU adoption and strong financial results.

Lower interest rates are supposed to be good news for technology stocks and crypto. But there is a wrinkle in the AI boom: The companies building the infrastructure are increasingly borrowing long-term to buy assets that can become obsolete far faster. That turns the bond market into an increasingly important test of the AI spending thesis.

Lee Sees Easier Money Ahead

Fundstrat’s Tom Lee expects bond yields to normalize over the next six months as inflation pressures ease, arguing that technology stocks and crypto are already signaling easier financial conditions ahead. He said a 10-year Treasury yield below 5% would be "really positive for risk-on."

The equity-market logic is straightforward. Lower yields reduce the cost of borrowing and increase the value investors place on future earnings, potentially giving high-growth technology stocks another tailwind.

But the AI infrastructure boom creates a complication.

The world’s largest technology companies are no longer funding all that growth from their own cash flow. Amazon.com Inc (NASDAQ:AMZN), Microsoft Corp (NASDAQ:MSFT), Alphabet Inc (NASDAQ:GOOGL)(NASDAQ:GOOG), Meta Platforms Inc (NASDAQ:META) and Oracle Corp (NYSE:ORCL) issued roughly $200 billion of investment-grade debt during the first half of 2026, almost twice their issuance during all of 2025, according to iShares.

AI Is Becoming a Bond Trade

Oracle provides perhaps the clearest example. The company said it expects to raise $45 billion to $50 billion in gross cash during 2026 through a combination of debt and equity to expand its cloud infrastructure for customers including Advanced Micro Devices, Inc. (NASDAQ:AMD), Meta, Nvidia Corp. (NASDAQ:NVDA), OpenAI and xAI.

Alphabet has also been spending at extraordinary levels. The company spent $80.6 billion on capital expenditures during the first half of 2026, more than double the $39.6 billion spent during the comparable period a year earlier. Its long-term debt stood at $98.2 billion at the end of June.

The issue isn’t necessarily that this spending is reckless. AI infrastructure can generate revenue for years, and companies such as Alphabet and Oracle have substantial existing businesses supporting their balance sheets.

The question is duration.

Some of the GPUs being purchased for today’s AI buildout can have an economic life of roughly two to three years before newer, more powerful chips make them less competitive for the most demanding workloads. That creates an unusual financing mismatch: A hyperscaler could be paying off a 10-year bond long after the two-year-old hardware it helped finance has been replaced or relegated to less demanding uses.

A data center may be financed with debt lasting a decade or more, while the computing hardware inside it can have a much shorter economic life as AI chips become faster and more efficient.

Read Also: AI’s $1 Trillion Funding Problem Is Moving From Stocks to Bonds

The Bond Market Wants Proof

That mismatch is becoming harder for investors to ignore. Goldman Sachs expects the five hyperscalers to issue roughly $250 billion of bonds this year and $400 billion in 2027.

At the same time, the 10-year Treasury yield has moved above 5%, raising the cost of capital even for companies with investment-grade credit. Reuters reported that investors are demanding higher yields as hyperscaler borrowing grows.

For equity investors, that creates a crucial test for the AI trade. If rates fall, Lee’s argument gets stronger. But if AI capex keeps rising faster than the cash flows it generates, lower rates may simply make it easier to finance an even larger infrastructure bill.

That makes the next phase of the AI trade less about whether companies can borrow and more about whether the returns from those billions in GPUs, data centers and power infrastructure arrive before the debt comes due.

Investors should watch free cash flow, capex guidance and borrowing costs together—not in isolation.

A 32-gigawatt power shortfall could delay America’s AI data-center boom, but Nvidia Corp. (NASDAQ:NVDA) and Broadcom Inc. (NASDAQ:AVGO) may be surprisingly well protected, according to Morgan Stanley.

Morgan Stanley estimates U.S. data-center developers face a 34% net power shortfall through 2028, equivalent to 32 gigawatts, even after accounting for workarounds such as fuel cells and power generated directly at data-center sites, according to Reuters.

The bank does not see the bottleneck putting Nvidia or Broadcom’s 2027 forecasts at risk. Instead, some of the pain could move further down the semiconductor supply chain.

Why Nvidia and Broadcom May Be Protected

Morgan Stanley pointed to the companies’ visibility into where chips are being deployed, geographic expansion and coordination with data centers and the power industry. That could let Nvidia send scarce GPUs to projects that have power if one facility is delayed, while suppliers tied to that project may have less flexibility.

The bank has separately argued that Nvidia’s advantage increasingly comes down to computing output per gigawatt. If electricity becomes the constraint, customers have more reason to squeeze as much computing power as possible from every watt.

Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has described the bottleneck in similar terms, saying AI developers now need to “secure the land, power, and shell” before filling data centers with computing equipment. He said that process can take two to three years.

Nvidia is already backing that infrastructure, providing credit support for 4.25 GW at SB Energy’s Ohio campus and investing $1.5 billion in the developer.

A Memory Shortage Meets a Power Shortage

Morgan Stanley said delayed deployments could force customers to push out or cancel deliveries of memory, optical, power-management and analog components.

The bank did not specifically name Micron Technology Inc. (NASDAQ:MU), but its warning comes as the memory industry is telling investors a very different story.

Micron says more than 75% of its 2027 output is already committed, while investor Ross Gerber said the AI-driven memory shortage could last a decade.

The two views are not necessarily contradictory. Morgan Stanley is warning about when memory gets deployed, not whether AI will ultimately need it.

A data center delayed six months may still require the same memory, but customers could push out deliveries while they wait for electricity, creating inventory disruption even during a broader memory shortage.

Prediction traders aren’t betting on the power crunch breaking the AI boom yet. Polymarket puts the chance of an AI-industry downturn at about 7% by year-end and 19% by June 30, 2027.

A legal filing in Florida accuses pharmaceutical giant Pfizer Inc. (NYSE:PFE) and Chairman and CEO Albert Bourla of deceiving consumers by concealing critical safety risks and unverified transmission claims.

Who is Suing?

The lawsuit was filed by the Office of the Attorney General of the State of Florida (Department of Legal Affairs), on behalf of the State of Florida, led by Florida Attorney General James Uthmeier.

It alleges that Pfizer violated the Florida Deceptive and Unfair Trade Practices Act by misleading the public, hiding internal safety data, and disparaging concerned citizens.

Benzinga has reached out to Pfizer for comments and will update the story upon receiving their stance.

Florida Attorney General James Uthmeier has opposed the corporate marketing and forced mandates of the COVID-19 vaccine, publicly accusing drug manufacturers of concealing serious health risks.

Aggressive Marketing Campaign Drives Massive Revenue

According to the court document, Pfizer spent more than $10 billion on advertising from 2020 to 2023 to build consumer demand for its novel mRNA COVID-19 vaccine.

This extensive marketing push successfully generated over $80 billion in vaccine sales for the company. During this same period, Bourla earned nearly $102 million in compensation, supplemented by stock profits and book sales.

To secure these windfall profits, Pfizer executives conducted media appearances assuring Florida residents the vaccine was completely safe. Bourla publicly declared that the company had not observed a single safety signal.

Furthermore, Pfizer pressured consumers by asserting that mass vaccination was a moral duty required to prevent transmitting the virus to loved ones.

Complaint Alleges Concealed Safety Risks And Unverified Claims

However, the state lawsuit asserts Pfizer possessed internal data reflecting serious safety risks that were hidden from the public. These included links to myocarditis and pericarditis in minors, strokes, and elderly fatalities.

The complaint also highlights concerns over adverse events for pregnant women, including miscarriages, which were discussed among Anthony Fauci, Surgeon General Vivek Murthy, and CDC Director Rochelle Walensky.

The filing further claims Pfizer had never tested the vaccine’s effect on transmission when making those moral appeals to consumers.

Instead of offering full public transparency, Pfizer actively worked to quash opposition by branding skeptics as criminals, leveraging deceptive practices to protect corporate revenues at the expense of Florida consumers making sensitive medical choices.

That puts First Trust Nasdaq Clean Edge Smart Grid Infrastructure ETF (NASDAQ:GRID) at the center of the second-order AI trade. The ETF gained more than 19% year to date, outperforming its infrastructure category’s 14.85% return.

Quanta Services (NYSE:PWR), which Jim Cramer calls a “terrific” stock, accounts for 8.68% of the fund. Eaton (NYSE:ETN) represents 8.45%. Johnson Controls International PLC (NYSE:JCI), ABB (OTC:ABBNY) and Schneider Electric were also among its largest holdings.

Caterpillar itself reported a 24% jump in second-quarter revenue to $20.5 billion, with Power & Energy sales rising 17%; the company specifically cited higher sales of power-generation equipment in data-center applications.

AI’s next bottleneck may not be computing power — it may be the physical power needed to run it. And that could make infrastructure ETFs an increasingly important way to play the AI super-cycle without betting on a handful of mega-cap technology stocks.

On Thursday, authorities arrested a California man on federal charges alleging he helped smuggle more than $300 million worth of export-controlled computer servers reportedly containing Nvidia Corp. (NASDAQ:NVDA) GPUs to China without the required licenses.

California Man Faces Federal Export Charges

Greg Lui, 38, also known as Yiu Kong Lui, of San Gabriel, California, faces charges of conspiring to violate the Export Control Reform Act and Export Administration Regulations, outbound smuggling and conspiracy to commit money laundering.

According to the DOJ, Lui owns Earthmade Computer, a closely held technology company.

The company allegedly purchased and shipped export-controlled equipment to China between 2023 and 2024 without obtaining licenses from the U.S. Department of Commerce.

Prosecutors said Lui purchased 27 servers containing Nvidia H100 GPUs from an unidentified U.S. manufacturer for approximately $7.6 million under a single purchase order, The Straits Times reported.

"This case shows yet again that smuggling is a losing proposition–legally, economically and technically. Our work with law enforcement has led to prosecutions, and we will continue to engage with law enforcement,” an Nvidia spokesperson told Benzinga via email.

Prosecutors allege Lui and his co-conspirators routed the equipment through countries including Malaysia and Singapore, where the shipments did not require the same U.S. export licenses, before allegedly re-exporting the technology to China.

The servers contained graphics processing units, or GPUs, commonly used in artificial intelligence applications.

Countries Target AI Technology Shipments to China

The U.S. began restricting Nvidia’s advanced chip exports to China in 2022 and gradually expanded those controls.

Nvidia Corp. (NASDAQ:NVDA)–backed Reflection AI is stepping deeper into the global AI race with Beam, its first open-weight model designed to compete with lower-cost Chinese systems such as DeepSeek and Kimi in coding and agentic tasks.

Reflection AI Launches New Beam Model

The startup said Beam delivers performance comparable to Chinese AI firm Z.ai’s GLM-5.2 and is approaching the capabilities of Qwen3.8-Max in coding and agentic workloads.

Beam has 501 billion parameters, which are the variables that help an AI model process information. However, it activates only about 23 billion parameters for each task, potentially delivering large-model capabilities while using less computing power.

That compares with GLM-5.2, which has roughly 744 billion total parameters and activates about 40 billion at a time.

Beam’s Safety and Alignment

Reflection AI said it trained a separate safety model using supervised fine-tuning and reinforcement learning, then combined it with a large-scale RL model through multi-teacher distillation.

In a blog post, the company said, "We will publish the results of our safety evaluations in our model technical report and will open-source safety evaluations we developed and used internally to create a shared, inspectable standard that the open ecosystem can test against and contribute to."

Beam Targets China’s Low-Cost AI Models

Reflection’s launch comes as U.S. technology companies face growing competition from Chinese open-weight models that offer lower costs, greater customization and increasingly strong coding capabilities.

Open-weight models allow developers to access and modify a model’s trained weights, giving them more flexibility than closed systems that can only be accessed through a company’s platform.

Nvidia-Backed Startup Expands Computing Capacity

Founded in 2024 by former DeepMind researchers Misha Laskin and Ioannis Antonoglou, Reflection develops AI tools aimed at automating software development.

The company also secured a computing-capacity agreement with Space Exploration Technologies Corp. (NASDAQ:SPCX) earlier this year, giving it access to additional resources at SpaceX’s Colossus 2 data center.

Alphabet Inc. (NASDAQ:GOOG) (NASDAQ:GOOGL) is expanding its enterprise AI and cloud modernization push as Google looks to extract more value from legacy infrastructure. Meanwhile, investors are weighing that opportunity against intensifying competition in consumer AI and potential disruption to its core search business.

Google Targets Enterprise Modernization With AI

Google Cloud launched Google Cloud Modernize, an end-to-end portfolio designed to help enterprises speed up infrastructure, platform and application modernization using AI.

The portfolio combines existing migration tools, including Migration Center, Google Cloud VMware Engine and Google Cloud Mainframe Modernization, with newer offerings such as the EKS-to-GKE Migration Agent.

Google also launched Modernization Hub, an in-console platform that helps developers and architects analyze source code, map dependencies and modernize Java, .NET and mainframe applications.

In addition, Google is adding Gemini capabilities to Migration Center. Its Agentic Quick Estimator can turn VMware inventory and infrastructure data into total cost of ownership projections. That allows customers to test assumptions and identify potential savings.

Google said the tools can reduce weeks of spreadsheet modeling to minutes.

See More: Top Value Stocks

Google Expands Infrastructure for AI Workloads

Google also introduced infrastructure aimed at increasingly demanding enterprise workloads.

Its X5 Series supports SAP S/4HANA configurations with up to 43 TiB of memory. Meanwhile, the M4N Series targets database workloads and can cut software licensing costs by more than 20% for Oracle and other core-licensed databases.

Google also highlighted Z4D and Z4M systems for high-speed data workloads. In addition, it introduced a self-managed VMware option for organizations seeking cloud flexibility without immediately re-architecting existing environments.

The new EKS-to-GKE Agentic Migration offering automates transitions from Amazon.com Inc. (NASDAQ:AMZN) Amazon Web Services’ Elastic Kubernetes Service to Google Kubernetes Engine.

NetEase Games said using GKE reduced infrastructure scaling times from hours to five minutes during peak launches. It also cut server costs by 40%.

Alphabet Faces Pressure in Consumer AI

Despite Google’s enterprise push, Alphabet faces a tougher competitive landscape in consumer AI.

CNBC reported Friday that Alphabet shares gave up an initial gain after the launch of Gemini 4 Argon. The model posted strong coding and cybersecurity benchmarks, but its limited rollout gave investors little visibility into real-world performance.

Meta Platforms Inc. (NASDAQ:META) has also intensified the competition.

CNBC noted that Meta Muse has pushed the AI battle toward personal agents and accumulated an estimated more than 5 million downloads. Google’s Spark agent remains behind a paywall and cannot make calls or purchases for users.

JPMorgan said Google continues to release AI products but has yet to produce a breakout consumer hit, according to CNBC.

Meta shares have gained more than 20% over the past month, compared with about 3% for Alphabet.

Cloud Growth Remains a Key Opportunity

Google Cloud remains a major growth engine for Alphabet.

CNBC said Google’s Flash models helped support more than 80% year-over-year growth in Google Cloud during the most recent quarter.

Bank of America Securities views Gemini 4 Argon as more important for winning cloud business than driving consumer adoption, according to CNBC.

Google is also exploring whether Argon could power a revamped version of Spark.

AI Agents Could Challenge Search

The longer-term risk is that personal AI agents could change how consumers search, shop and book travel.

JPMorgan warned that agents capable of handling those tasks could bypass Google Search, potentially threatening Alphabet’s advertising business.

That leaves Alphabet balancing two forces. Google Cloud is creating new enterprise AI and modernization opportunities, while Meta’s progress in personal AI agents is increasing pressure on Google to turn its technological strength into broader consumer adoption.

Google’s ability to expand enterprise AI, strengthen Spark and defend Search will remain central to Alphabet’s growth outlook.

Microsoft Corp. (NASDAQ:MSFT) is pushing Copilot beyond a workplace chatbot and into a broader AI platform as it looks to drive new revenue across Microsoft 365 and Azure.

The strategy comes as Microsoft ramps up spending on data centers and computing capacity to meet surging AI demand. At the same time, higher Treasury yields are putting pressure on richly valued technology stocks.

Cramer Sees Microsoft Among AI Leaders

CNBC’s Jim Cramer said Monday that Microsoft is among a small group of AI leaders strong enough to help offset pressure from rising interest rates.

“Here, I think there’s tremendous distortion caused by some very big winners, namely NVIDIA Corp. (NASDAQ:NVDA), Microsoft and Meta Platforms Inc. (NASDAQ:META),” Cramer said.

He pointed to improving sentiment around Copilot as a key catalyst for Microsoft. NVIDIA continues to benefit from strong AI chip demand, while Meta is gaining momentum around its Muse personal AI agent.

Microsoft accounted for roughly 5.8% of the S&P 500 as of Friday’s close. That gives moves in the software giant an outsized influence on the broader index.

Microsoft Pushes Copilot Beyond Chat

Microsoft recently redesigned Copilot around Home, Code and Autopilot as it seeks to make the product a central interface for workplace AI.

Executive Vice President Jared Spataro said Microsoft wants Copilot to play a role in the AI era similar to Office during the PC era.

Home combines Chat and Cowork. Code allows users to create apps, dashboards and workflows using natural-language prompts. Autopilot can handle recurring and longer-running tasks within defined permissions and governance controls.

The shift could also broaden Microsoft’s monetization opportunities. The company plans to use subscriptions for everyday Copilot access while charging customers based on consumption for more compute-intensive workloads.

Microsoft also reportedly plans discounts of about 30% for customers buying more than 1,000 seats and as much as 50% for purchases above 10,000 seats.

Oppenheimer Sees Azure, Microsoft 365 Upside

Oppenheimer analyst Brian Schwartz said Microsoft’s latest Copilot strategy transforms the product from a chatbot into what he views as an AI operating system.

Schwartz said the shift could boost engagement, retention and monetization across Azure and Microsoft 365. He raised his Microsoft price forecast to $570 from $515 and named the stock a top pick.

The analyst also highlighted Microsoft’s multi-model strategy, which gives customers access to technology from OpenAI, Anthropic and Muse.

Azure is growing in the low-40% range, while Microsoft has guided for growth to accelerate into the mid-40% range this quarter. Schwartz believes growth approaching 50% at a business already exceeding $100 billion in scale could support a higher valuation.

AI Demand Tests Microsoft’s Computing Capacity

Microsoft is also racing to expand its data center footprint as AI workloads strain available computing capacity.

Bloomberg reported that Microsoft aims to increase data center capacity to more than 38 gigawatts by 2032 from about 12 gigawatts currently. However, a company spokesperson disputed those projections.

The shortage of available computing power has already forced Microsoft to limit some new cloud subscriptions and has pushed certain customers toward rivals, according to the report.

Microsoft spent $145 billion on capital expenditures in its latest fiscal year as it poured money into data centers, chips and other AI infrastructure.

That spending reflects a wider industry arms race. Goldman Sachs expects AI capital expenditures by major hyperscalers, including Microsoft, to rise more than 50% to $1.2 trillion in 2027.

For Microsoft, the challenge is turning that enormous infrastructure investment into sustained growth across Azure, Microsoft 365 and Copilot while demand for AI computing continues to outstrip available capacity.

NVIDIA Expands Buyback As Cash Generation Surges

NVIDIA’s board recently added $150 billion to its share repurchase authorization, bringing the remaining authorization to about $235 billion through fiscal 2028.

CEO Jensen Huang linked the expanded buyback to NVIDIA’s strong cash generation and confidence in what he has described as a broader “platform shift to AI and accelerated computing.”

At the same time, NVIDIA is expanding beyond chips and computing infrastructure.

The company launched its Open Agent Safety Platform to help enterprises monitor and control autonomous AI agents. More than 100 organizations are working with NVIDIA’s agent-safety technologies, including Anthropic, Salesforce Inc. (NYSE:CRM) and SAP SE (NYSE:SAP).

Huang has also argued that AI infrastructure demand continues to accelerate as companies generate more tokens, deploy increasingly complex models and expand computing capacity.

Dan Ives Says Estimates May Be Too Low

Yorkville Ives partner Dan Ives told CNBC on Tuesday that Wall Street may still be significantly underestimating NVIDIA’s growth trajectory.

“I think investors are realizing numbers are probably underestimated by 25, 30% over the next year,” Ives said.

He pointed to accelerating enterprise AI adoption and extremely tight supply-demand conditions, particularly across Asia.

“Demand vs. supply, 13 to 1, 14 to 1,” Ives said.

He added that new use cases, including physical AI, are broadening NVIDIA’s opportunity beyond traditional data-center customers.

“There’s one chip in the world fueling it, and that’s NVIDIA,” Ives said.

Ives argued that investors may be underestimating NVIDIA not only for the current quarter, but across the next six to eight quarters as AI spending expands.

Enterprise AI Adds Another Growth Engine

Ives also tied NVIDIA’s outlook to rising spending from hyperscalers and enterprise customers.

He pointed to Microsoft Corp. (NASDAQ:MSFT) and the expansion of Azure AI workloads as part of the broader NVIDIA demand story. Microsoft and other technology giants continue to pour capital into data centers, GPUs and related infrastructure.

Huang has made a similar argument from the infrastructure side.

He estimated that a 1-gigawatt NVIDIA-powered AI facility can cost roughly $50 billion to $60 billion to build and generate about $50 billion in annual rental revenue under current market conditions.

Huang also said Grace Blackwell systems can command rental rates of about $16 per GPU hour, compared with roughly $5 under some contracts signed a year earlier. The increase highlights the strength of demand for advanced AI computing capacity.

Buyback Adds to Bullish Case

Highline Asset Management Managing Director Ben Emons also pointed to NVIDIA’s buyback as a signal of management’s confidence in the company’s long-term outlook.

“NVIDIA’s buyback announcement was a bright spot,” Emons wrote. “The buyback is not just a payout but a capital-allocation event that asserts confidence in long-run AI demand.”

NVIDIA’s enormous market value also gives the stock growing influence over the broader market. The company represents about 13% of the Nasdaq-100 and roughly 8% of the S&P 500.

The biggest question is whether NVIDIA can continue delivering growth strong enough to justify expectations that are already exceptionally high.

Ives believes it can. He sees demand continuing to outstrip supply as hyperscaler spending, enterprise AI, physical AI and new workloads expand NVIDIA’s addressable market.

Bitcoin (CRYPTO: BTC) whales have added $1.22 billion since Oct/ 1, fueling what one analyst calls a lockout rally toward $100,000.

What a ‘Lockout Rally’ Means

John Gillen, host of the Milk Road crypto podcast, explained on Monday’s show that Bitcoin has been in a lockout rally since August. 

Price moves sideways in a tight range, volatility shrinks, and then it jumps higher. As a result, buyers never get a clean entry. 

He argues that six to nine months of deep fear already pushed casual traders out of the market, which leaves few sellers. 

Even a 15% to 25% drop would not change his plan to keep buying. “I’m long as hell,” he told viewers

Why Crypto Is Rising While Stocks Stall

John said the rally rests on adoption and regulation, not a short squeeze. He pointed to three recent developments that give more investors access to crypto:

  • SEC innovation exemption: lets companies tokenize U.S. stocks for five years
  • OKX and the New York Stock Exchange: plan to put more than 60 tokenized stocks on OKX’s X Layer network
  • Leveraged ETFs: the SEC approved its first 3x leveraged Bitcoin and Ethereum (CRYPTO: ETH) ETFs this week

John does not see the recovery as stretched, because Bitcoin at $85,000 sits only slightly above its average price for the past year. 

He reads the move as a return to normal after a deep selloff, not an overvalued market.

He rejected a viral cycle theory that called for a market bottom on October 6, one year after Bitcoin’s high near $126,000, because markets do not follow a set number of days. 

That view matches investor Dan Tapiero’s post, who called $100,000 a “chip shot” from here.

Why Yet Another Analyst Sees $100,000

Widely-followed crypto analyst Ali Martinez posted a thread on X showing that Bitcoin has traded between $83,000 and $86,700 for two weeks. 

He cited Glassnode data showing 1.59 million BTC changed hands between $83,300 and $84,600, which gives buyers a zone to defend. 

Above $86,700, the same data shows no comparable cluster of coins until about $105,000.

Santiment data in the thread also shows that large holders added more than 14,335 BTC, worth about $1.22 billion, since Oct. 1.

What Could Interrupt the Rally

John warned that bond yields, the standoff over the Strait of Hormuz and the U.S. midterms could bring turbulence in October. 

A 10% pullback in the S&P 500 (NYSE:SPY) could also drag Bitcoin lower according to him, though that has not happened yet.

Key Levels for Bitcoin

Martinez said $100,000 could return to focus if buyers defend support and clear the top of the range:

  • $86,700: breakout point and top of the two-week range
  • $83,300 to $84,600: support zone

Meta Platforms Inc. (NASDAQ:META) is facing a U.K. investigation into whether Instagram’s new Instants feature received adequate safety checks before its launch.

The U.K.’s communications watchdog Ofcom is examining whether Meta breached Britain’s Online Safety Act by failing to properly assess risks connected to Instants, according to a press release.

Instagram Instants lets users send disappearing images that vanish after being viewed. The feature blocks forwarding and includes protections tied to Instagram’s teen-account settings.

The regulator is evaluating whether the feature could expose users to illegal content or allow children to access material that presents safety concerns. The investigation does not establish that Meta violated the law.

Ofcom can issue warnings or impose fines of up to 10% of a company’s global revenue in case of a security breach. The regulator is separately investigating Meta over an alleged failure to provide information involving WhatsApp.

The Mark Zuckerberg-led company told the Guardian that it conducted a risk assessment and consulted Ofcom before launching Instants, adding protections such as blocking forwarding and applying all standard teen-account safeguards for users under 18.
